analysis.title: About Last Night: The "Blue Wave" Makes Landfall in U.S. Midterms
key_insights: Democrats won both chambers in the U.S. midterms. They hold at least 236 House seats (projected about 257 once votes are finalized, from 214 before, 218 needed) and at least 54 Senate seats (from 47, up to 56 possible, 51 needed). Results exceeded model expectations.
Senate flips include former long-time Republican strongholds in South Carolina, Kansas and Texas. Democrats also won governors' races, including historic wins in Texas and Georgia.

The author attributes much of the outcome to high gas prices and higher costs of living, which have ousted incumbents of all leanings in elections globally. The author cautions against reading the result purely as a referendum on the President.

Equities fell overnight as the result became clear. The stated reasons were more regulatory scrutiny of AI weighing on Information Technology, slower deregulation elsewhere, and reduced spending that means a smaller fiscal impulse (the $5,000 cheques are unlikely to be sent).

The selloff broadly reversed at the open. Investors appear to view gridlock and a Congress that restrains the Administration's less market-friendly policies as positive, and expect solid underlying economic momentum to continue.
Congress acting as a counterbalance to the White House could be a recurring market theme over the next two years.
Markets have been higher one year after every midterm in the post-WWII era, even though they often react adversely to political changeovers.

Treasuries are bid on the prospect that government pushback on added spending helps fiscal sustainability. Moves in crude and inflation break-evens suggest part of the move reflects hopes for a quick resolution in the Middle East that relieves inflationary pressure.
A new Congress may open the door to a less combative relationship with Canada and others and some easing on tariffs, though this is undetermined.
Congress does not convene until January 3, 2027. Republicans can push agenda items through the lame duck session, after which passing legislation becomes much harder for the President.
